In the vicinity of the village, there\nis one of those Lamaist gates built across the road, such as are frequently met with in\nthese parts. (Plate T, b.) In Ladakh there are many similar ones. They all have a\nmckod-rten on the roof, and frescoes on the ceiling. Here in the Kanawari country these\n-are distinguished by their elegant wooden roofs which are built over the tnchod-rten, to\nprotect it from rain. The roof is covered, and, therefore, has somewhat the appearance of\na Chinese roof. Gerard believed all this kind of arobitectui*e to be influenced by the\nChinese style of building, which he believed to exist immediately on tbe other side of the\nTibeto-OMnese frontier. However, we should have to travel thousands of miles, before\nwe should meet with the first representatives of Chinese architecture. These doors are\nhere known by tbe name of kang-ga-ni, a name which is given in Ladakh only to the\nmost ancient specimens.\n\nClose to the door, there are two large erect stones, perhaps rude specimens of lingmis. They have carvings on them, which I copied. One of the carvings I take for a kind\nof sun-symbol. It was very distinct on one of tbe stones. On the other stone was carved\na stupa and what appears to be a repetition of the sun-symbol.\n\nAt Pangi, I met Mr. Bruske and his wife, who were encamped there. I spent a fewpleasant hours with them, and received much valuable information from them.\n\nWe spent the night of tbe 29th and the 30th June at Barang. In the evening, w'e\nvisited the Lamaist temple, which is built somewhat in the style of the wooden hill\n\n1 See my Iiitroduction to Ladakhi Songs, In^. Ant, Yol. XXXI. 1902. pp. 87\n\narchitecturej at least in regard to its roof. It is said to be only about twenty-five yearsold. In the courtyard, we found cremation tablets with figures of AvaloMte^vara\nre|)resented with four arms and a lotus, and Hi-uhJiTugs-pti’ (Akshobya). Although they\nwere also said to be of recent date, the mould from which they were cast must be\ndecidedly old. It was possibly brought here from Kanam monastery, which claims to be\nold. The tablets were furnished with Tibetan inscriptions, but these were so indistinct\nthat nothing could be read. It was just possible to see that the characters employed\nwere Tibetan.\n\nAbove the village of Rarang, on the road, there is an old hut which is known as the\nmost ancient mandir of Rarang. (Plate VII, b.) It is rectangular, and has a slanting\nroof. The door beams are furnished with wood carvings. On the lintel, the figure of\nan elephant carrying a human being can be distinguished. This is possibly a representation of Indra. Of particular interest is the gable-roof which ends in the carving of a\nram’s head, and thus reminds us strongly of the devatd-hvits in the Manchad valley\n(Lahul). In its general appearance also, this mandir resembles the devatd-hxits of the\nManchad valley and goes to prove that the religion of the Kanawaris was similar to that of\nthe Manchad people, who are closely related to them by lingual and ethnic characteristics.\nAs this hut is practically the last specimen of Indian hill architecture on the road (not\ntaking into account a ‘ gate of blessing ’ at Poo, which is furnished wnth a roof in Kanawari style), it will be well to review all the observations w^'e have made with regard to\nthis arohiteotm’e. Under hill architecture are comprised all the structures which arc\ncomposed of rubble masonry and beams of cedar wood. Of an entirely different character are the structures of the Tibetans, which consist of sun-dried bricks. The former have\nslanting, and the latter flat roofs. On the frontier between the Tibetan and Xanawari\npeoples there are also some intermediate forms. There are houses built of rubble masonry\nwith flat roofs, for instance the temple at Rogi, and houses built of sun-burnt bricks with\na slanting roof, for instance the temple at Rarang.\n\nThe most elementary form of hill architecture is represented by the ancient mandir\nof Rarang, which consists of a one-roomed house with a rectangular ground-plan a.ud a\nslanting roof. Later on, the roof assumed a concave appearance, and was often supported\nby a covered verandah. This type of house is much in evidence as the ordinary\npeasant’s dwelling on the Satluj up to the Wangiu bridge, and the Nirmand temples are\nof this type. It was then modified in the following way. The ground plan was made\nsquare and the walls were raised. This is the type of the Kulu castle towers which were\nintroduced even into Lahul, and of the shrine of the old mandir at Urni, A beautiful\ncombination of this rectangular house and square tower is found in the ancient palace of\nSarahan. This we find in its simplest form in the modem temple of Urni, and in.\n\n. Site of Thakur’s castle, Chini. b' Shrine of Devi, Rarang.\n\none of tlie old temples of Sungra. Then there arose the custom of building with\nsuperimposed pyramidal roofs one on the top of another, the ujoper ones decreasing in\nsize ; the whole structures reminding us of Burmese Pagodas. The same must be said with regard to\nthe snake and bird ornaments which are frequently met with. The continual warfare\nbetween Garudas and Nagas was a favourite topic among the liiU tribes long before the rise\nof Buddhism. Rejoresentations of the human figure are also of frequent occurrence\namong these wood carvings. But they are by far inferior to the representations of\nanimals and look very much like the effigies of men on ancient rock carvings. The\ntypes are stiff and conventionalised, as if on the way to become pictographs. The wooden\neaves-boards which are often seen on the edges of roofs, form a very pretty kind of\nornament. Many of the roofs or gable beams end in dragon heads with oj)en mouths.\nOf the rams’ heads at the end of such beams mention has been made.\n\nWe passed through Jangi on the 30th June. Tibetan mani walls are now becoming\nfrequent, but up to this place they contained nothing beyond endless repetitions of the\nOm mani padnie 1mm. Here I found for the first time on our expedition a mani wall\nwith a votive tablet on one end. This shows that the knowledge of the Tibetan language\nis more general here than in the previous villages. The tablet was, however, so much\nworn that I could not read much beyond the wmrds Khungs-Usim-ga-ga-che, “ the great\nnobleman of excellent origin.” Neither this nor any of the preceding mani walls look\nas if they were of great antiquity. In the district between Ohini and Poo Lamaism has\nmade progress in outward show during the last thirty years or so without, however, ousting Hinduism.\n\nOpposite Jangi lies the village of Kinam with a fine castle on a rock above the river.\nIt was built, it is said, by the Raja of Bashahr.\n\nAfter Jangi, the country begins to show a Tibetan character. Vegetation becomes very\nscarce, and only a kind of Juniper, generally known by the name of Pencil Cedar (the\nholy tree of the pre-Buddhist religion of Tibet) makes us realize that we are not travelling on the moon. The pencil cedar never forms forests, but at best dots a hillside with\na tree to every 500 square yards or so. But the village as well as the monasteiy\npresents a purely Tibetan appearance. This monastery (Plate VIII) was the first on the\nroad which by the natives themselves was asserted to be of ancient origin. The monastery consists of three separate\nhalls situated in different parts of the village.\n\nThe uppermost of them is called dOon-pa or monastery proper. It is a building of the\nordinary Tibetan type, constructed of undried bricks with a flat roof. It contains the\ncells of the lamas who belong to the Ge-lug-pa sect, and an insignificant temple. In the\nlatter is found an image of Buddha, gilt bronze with blue hair of the pin-head type. The chief attraction of the Kanam monastery\nlies in the fact that the pioneer of Tibetan studies, the Hungarian Osoma de Kovos spent\nseveral years in it, studying the Tibetan language. The chief attraction of the little village of Kanam, for Csoma, rested in the fact
that the monastery contains complete copies of the IM-ngyur and bstan-ugywr, the great

^ See Duka, Idfe of Csoma^ pp. 82 ff .

Plate VIII.

b. Lotsabai Monastery, Kanam.

encyclopsedias of Lamaism. It ■was here that he was enabled to study these gigantic
collections of Tibetan literature, and to write his still inyaluable ‘ Analysis of the Eanjur
and Stanjur.’ The library is kept in a separate building called bM-tigyiir some distance
below the monastery, Gerard who inspected this library on the occasion of his visit to
Csoma in Kanam, has the following note on it : “ The edition of the Kahgym’ and Stan-

gyur at Kanum was sent from Teshi Ihunpo (bKra-shis-lhun-po) only about 9 years ago
{i.e. in 1820) ; the printing bears a date of ninety years, yet the ink and type look as
perfect and fresh as ever. No insects attack them, though the climate here is varying

in summer. The book cases being made of cedar are indestructible The works, being

distinct, are arranged in separate places. These resemble large chests or cisterns, standing on end, and partitioned into cells, each containing a volume, which is carefully
wrapped within many folds, laced with cord, and bound tightly between boards of cypress

or cedar Some of the volumes were opened before me, and I gazed with a sort of

reverential feeling upon such gigantic compilations yet unfolded to the world, and
thought of the humble individual in the hamlet who was occupied in illustrating their
unexplored contents.”

There is yet a third Lamaist building in the place. It is called Lliahrang and is
situated between the village and the fields. It is said to be of not much later date than
the dGon-pa. No ancient relic has been preserved in it. It contains a modern stucco
statue of Maitreya. Another small stucco statue represents the white Tara and is
believed to be of some antiquity. It is a really good piece of workmanship, and the face
shows expressive features, more spiritual than usual.

Above the d Qon-pa, there is a long row of white quadrangular bmldings which are
said to be crematories. In most villages, a single such incinerator has to suffice for many
people. Here one once used for a high lama, is apparently not used again. It is converted into a kind of quadrangular mchod-rten.

Although no ancient remains can be found at Kanam, it is quite possible that, as
asserted, a Lamaist monastery was built here in the 11th century. The present buildings
were probably erected on the sites of still more ancient ones. The monastery may have
-been ransacked several times ; for the last time by the Gurkhas. When Gerard was on
his expedition in the Satluj valley, he met with continual reports of the devastations by the Gurkhas from Kotgur to the Tibetan frontier.

On the 1st of July we marched from Kanam to the Shasu rope bridge. I arrived
at the bridge at 11 a.m., but did not reach the opposite bank of the river, a tributary to
the Satluj, before 6 p.m. When I arrived at the site of the bridge, nothing could be
seen but a steel rope. We had sent intimation of our intention to cross the bridge to the
next village, but there was no response. I found only a single old man on our bank of the
river, who had a one-wheeled trolley without any ropes at hand. When all our coolies had
come up and enjoyed a little rest, the ropes which they had used for carrying our bags and
boxes, were tied together and fastened to the trolley, and after much experimenting
it was found possible to work it, and our boxes one after another were slowly pulled across.

D

Ttea one of the ropes broke, just as one of the bags was right in the middle of the steel
rope, and we spent a very exciting time in watching two daring youths who waded through
the strong current, up to their chins, until they found the broken end of the rope. Having finally reached the other bank, it was night, and there being no time nor room to
-pitch tents, we had our beds in the open air and slept very comfortably.

W e arrived at Poo on the 2nd of July, after a tiring march over a hoirible road of very
rugged and unstable foundation mostly along the face of the precipice. There were hardly
any more Pencil cedar trees {Jmiperm excelsa) on the road. The scenery was now quite
Tibetan in character. Bad as the road was, the Missionary at Poo told me that it was
excellent compared to what it had been only five years ago. Honour to the brave Mission
ladies who have travelled on it in its old state ! 1 he rocks are dangerous, even to the natives.

About an hour before reaching Poo, the valley widens a little, and it is a relief to
be able to walk here without continuahy looking out for a safe foothold. Poo is situated
on a plain on the right bank of the Satluj and looks very pretty with its green fields,
apricot and apple tree gardens. Its elevation is about 9,500 feat, and it is the first village on our road, the language of which is entirely Tibetan. It looks as if it was entirely
closed in by steep bare mountains."

None of them seemed\nto be very ancient. The inscriptions consisted generally of four parts. The first part\nmay be called devotional, the second part consisted of a eulogy of the country of which\nthe village of Poo (spelled sP« in the inscriptions) was the centre, the third part j)raised\nthe Raja of Bashahr who was reigning at the time, and the fourth part contained the\naccount of the building of the wall, and stated for whose religious benefit it was meant.\nAs regards the names of Bashahr Rajas on the tablets, only the following four have\nbeen traced through Mr. Schnabel’s and our own combined efforts : Rudar (in Tibetan\nLurdur) Singh ; Ugar (in Tibetan TJrhu) Singh ; Mahindar (in Tibetan Metar) Siiigh •\nShamsher (in Tibetan ‘ golden thought ’) Siiigh. These names cover about\n\ntue last century. But there are some more mayii waUs with votive tablets which instead\n0 giving the proper name of a chief simply speak of ‘ the great king ’ at Sarahan (S'o-rarmff in Tibetan). This shows that the personal names of the rulers of Bashahr previous\n\ngeographical part (the\n\nvld the btderT these inscriptions, it contained many references to pkces be-\n\nOne of them is 'FJio i^^^ar interest are the clan names occurring in these inscriptions,\nof part of tko Poo ^pvoatio” ^\n\n~ “\n\nI Tras told that there rras an inscribed stone in the village of dKor, below Poo, and\nwent to examine it. Although the stone was generally known, nobody, not even the\nlamas, had tried to read it. The village of dKor is situated on the right bank of the\nlittle brook of Poo. The stone was found in a field belonging to a lama called hKa-rgyud\nIt is about six feet high. The upper half of the sculpture shows a well executed representation of a stupa, the lower half that of a human being. This part of the stone is\nin very bad preservation and most of it underground. The human figure wears a threepointed hat. On the reverse of the stone is a Tibetan inscription of eleven lines. Only\nthe first two lines are in fair preservation ; of all the other lines only the beginning and\nend have been preserved, whilst the middle part of those lines has been obliterated.\nWhile we were examining the stone, a Christian Tibetan who was with us, began to read\n\nthe first lines ; cl^al-lha-htsaii-po‘Llia-bla-ma-Ye-shes When he had got so far, I\n\nsuddenly remembered that I had heard of a person whose name began Llia-hla-nm- Ye-slies.\nBut what was the syllable following after Te-shes? It suddenly flashed on me, that it\nwas ’ofZ, and that hlia-bla-ma-Te-sJies-od was the name of the royal priest, the early\nking of Guge, who had tried in vain to draw the famous Buddhist monk Atiia to his\nkingdom. Did the inseriiition really contain his name — a name which has not yet been\ntraced anywhere ? We all went close to the stone, and looked at it from all sides, even\nfrom below. And lo, it was so. The stone contained the full name of this famous\npersonage of Tibetan liistory (c. 1025 A.D.) and the words following the name were\nsku-rmg-la, meaning ‘in his life time.’ I was so overjoyed at the discovery of this\nimportant record that I could not help jumping about in the field, and then embraced the\nlama, who was just ou the point of becoming displeased with my treatment of his crop.\n\nThe story of King Te-shes-’od is found in the second part of the Tibetan historical\nwork dTag-hsam-ljon-bzang, and a translation has been published by Sarat Chandra Das.^\nUp to the present, nobody had known whether the story contained in those works was\nreally true and whether the persons mentioned in it had actually lived or not. This site is lower\nthan most of the houses of Poo, and as an object of sanctity could not he suffered to stand\non a lower elevation than ordinary houses, a new temple was built higher up, in the\ncentre of Poo, and embell ished with the furnishings of the old one.\n\n^ Indian Tandits in the Land of ^now^ pp. 61 .\n\nD %\n\nThis temple, the oldest of the existing temples of Poo, is called Lo-tsa-hd-Lha-hhang\n■and is asserted to hare been built by Lo-tsa-ba Rin-ehen-bzang-po (Eatna-bhadra), the\nspiritual adviser of King Ye-shes-’od. The site was covered all over with large undressed stones, such as people still\n-use for building purposes. This part of the country was\nformerly under Guge and Ladakh, and, as in Ladakh, people were here also compelled to\nlive in fortified places on hilltops round their chief’s stronghold.\n\nThe deserted fields are locally known by the name Khola-ring.   "passage_text": "^ A class of deity which is of great fame at Poo and surrounding districts are the dd-ra-lJia who are also mentioned in the\nShar-rgan songs. As Mr. Schnabel tells me, there are nine dGra41ia of different names said to exist in nine villages vi\nUpper Kanawar. They are the following : Khro-mo-min, at Poo ; Chags-drid at Kanam ; lPahlim-lzang-7m at Dabling ;\n<Clios4ha Izang-rig-fa, at Pobbaling ; Tsa-hJiang at Lid or Sarkhung ; Kin \"ahrug hJcra-&liis, at Shasu ; Judi-dung^mo,\natKhab; gSergen-chen-po, atNamgja; dMag-gi-dpon-^po^ Six of them are of the male, and three of them,\n\n-those at Poo, Dabling, and Khab, are of the female sex.\n\nTibetans. The Tibetans practised human sacrifices, but for different motives from what\nwe have obseryed in the Satluj valley. Oaths at important treaties were emphasised by\nhuman as well as animal sacrifices. New houses were inaugurated by immuring human\nbeings and a person was killed when a house was first inhabited.^ Thus, at the village of\nPoo, a lama had only recently beheaded his own father while asleep, to make the new\nhouse he had built, properly habitable.\n\nThe Shar-rgan sacrifices as well as the human sacrifices in the Satluj valley and in\nLahul are of a very different character. To understand them, it is necessary to investigate the character of the deities in whose honour they are celebrated. Siva and Kali, as\nwe find them in the Himalayas, are personifications of the creative powers ; they do not\nonly j)roduce the harvest of the fields, but also bless the women with children, especially\nsons. In this respect, the principal deities of the pre- Buddhist religion of the Tibetans,\nin particular Ke-sar and ’aBru-gu-ma, resemble Siva and Kali. For as I have shown\npreviously,^ Ke-sar and ’aBru-gu-ma were both invoked by the people to grant children.\nThis explains the union which was formed between the Tibetan pre-BudJhist and the\naboriginal Siva-Kali religion, as we find it represented in the Shar-rgan hymnal. (The\nword shar-rgan means “ young and old ”.) But Ke-sar and ’aBru-gu-ma M^ere not of the\nfierce character of §iva and Kali. The latter were only ready to grant a blessing, when\na portion of what they had given, was returned to them. Hence not only a portion of\nthe harvest of the fields, or some of the Iambs of the flock had to be returned to them in\nsacrifice, but they also claimed some of the children with whom they had blessed the\nvillage. Almost invariably the traditions speak of children who were sacrificed. Here\nat Poo, the sacrifice had to be made on the occasion of a festival which is still now-a-days\nrecognised as a festival or thanksgiving for the blessing of offspring. In Lahul, the\nprayer on the occasion of such sacrifices was apparently intended more as a thanksgiving\nfor a good harvest in the fields.\n\nThe old Shar-rgan place is exactly above the site of the ancient castle of Kalagtrung\nand probably belonged to it. The new Shar-rgan place is situated a little above the road\nfrom Poo to Eizhing. At the latter place, there are a few old pencil-cedars, and a number\nof rough altars, furnished with horns of goats and wild antelopes, and pencil-cedar twigs.\nThey look exactly like the lha-tho of Ladakh. A third place which is connected with the\nsame festival is found in the middle of the village of Poo, and is called Dralang {sGralang (?) ‘ raising the voice ’) . It is used for dancin g and has a pole in the middle. On two\nsides of the place, there are lha-tho like those on the new Shar-rgan place, and two perpendicular stones, one showing traces of an inscription seemingly Om-a-hwk. The\nother plain one is probably a rude kind of lihgam, like those in Manchad. Not far\nfrom it, there are holes or pits where again children used to be sacrificed. (Plate\nIX. b).\n\nThe people of Poo although they are Buddhists, do not always cremate their dead,\nbut bury them in certai n cases. There are two burial places outside the village, one for\n\n* The Dard Bridge, see my Eistory of Western Tibet. = Z. B, M, G., Vol. LXI, pp. 683 ff.\n\nmore respectable peoj)le, as Mr. Scliiiabel informed me, the other one for poor peo 2 >lo\nand such, as die of infectious diseases. The graves consist of rocks and stones above the\nground. Some corpses are even thrown into the river, especially those of peojde who die\nof dropsy. Do the people of Poo believe that the accumulation of water in the body of\na sick person is a sign that the Nagas {Klu) claim the body ?\n\nBefore leaving Poo, I consider it necessary to write a short note about the line of kings\n■who reigned herein former days. As has already been stated, King Ye-shes-’od, whose\ninscription we discovered at Poo, reigned at mTho-lding, the old caj)ital of Griige, in the\ndays of the great teacher Atl^a. Now a king of the same name is mentioned among the\ndescendants of the first king of Zangskar, and closer research reveals the fact that the\nZangskar kings actually reigned at mTho-lding in G-uge. How is this to be accounted\nfor ? My explanation is this : King Nyi-ma-mgon of Western Tibet divided his empire\namong his three sons. The eldest received Ladakh, the second received Guge and Purang with mTho-lding as his caj)ital, the third one’s portion was Zangskar. The histori-\n•cal accounts of the Tibetans relate of descendants of the first and third sons, but they do\nnot give any names of descendants of the second son. There were apparently none.\nThe king of Guge and Puraug died ■without issue. Then his country was seized by the\nking of Zangskar, whose sway thereby extended over Zangskar, Guge and Purang, and\nwhose glory almost echpsed that of the kings of Leh. Ye-shes-’od is a member of the\nimportant line of kings who reigned over the three countries mentioned above and whose\ncapital was at mTho-lding."

  "passage_text": "We left Poo on the 6th July on our way to Shij)ke, At first our road took us\n•down to the rocky banks of the Satluj where we had to cross a rope bridge. The\nplace of this bridge is called mTho-rang, or ‘ Height itself.’ Prom inscriptions on\nboth banks of the river, it becomes evident that there has been a bridge in this jplace\nfrom ancient times. The oldest insorij)tion is in Gupta characters, and too much\neffaced to allow of reading more than sya, the termination of the genitive case, at the end\ncf the line. Several of the Tibetan inscriptions seem to be ! almost a thousand years of age,\njudging by the form of their characters. It is interesting to note that two of them, one\non each bank of the river, give the following advice to the j)erson who intends crossing :\nMa-ni-grongs-sUg ! “ Do not forget the mani (the Oih vmyii padme Mm) [when crossing]”!\nThis was very appropriate advice, for unpleasant as this bridge is now-a-days, it was far\nmore unpleasant in the old days when the traveller had to entrust his life to three rotten\nropes plaited of willow twigs at an altitude of about 100 feet above a broad and violent\nstream. No wonder, people called the bridge ‘ Height itself. ’ At the present day, - the\nbridge consists of a strong steel cable provided by the Public Works Department;\nand the usual trolley being broken, a wooden saddle with two rope slings attached to it,\nhas to do service instead. As Mr. Schnabd informs me, hardly a year passes by without\naccidents on this bridge, and even a battered traveller like Sven Hedin -who had to cross it\nten months before us, clothed his feelings in the words : “ This bridge is a proper place\nfor people desirous of committing suicide ! ”\n\nWe arrived at the village of Namgya (spelt sNam-rgya in an historical document) on\nthe 6th July, after a hot march over very uneven groundJ Soon after our arrival, the\nvillage chief, called Hira, made his appearance and entered into conversation with me.\nHe said, he was a descendant of a Tibetan family of hlon-po, ministers, who had formerly\nbeen in charge of this district, and indeed, he had quite the bearing of a gentleman. In\nthe course of our conversation he exhibited an extraordinary knowledge of things historical, in particular with regard to the battle of Basgo in 1646-47 A.D When I ex-\npressed my astonishment at such wisdom, he said that he was in possession of a document\nof ancient times. After much persuasion he produced it, and it turned out to be a copy\nof the treaty between Raja Kehari Singh {Kyeris Sing in Tibetan) of Bashahr and the\nLhasa Government, headed by Galdan Thsang (Thse-dbang). This Galdan Thsang is the\nvery general of the Tibeto- Mongolian army who had conducted the siege of Basgo. Of\nthis most important document, I ordered a copy to he made at once and offered Rl for\nit I said that I expected to get the copy on our way hack from Shipke in a few days,\nto which the old gentleman consented. On our way back, I had to find out, however,\nthat Hira was no longer a gentleman, as he would not hand over the copy, until he had\nextorted E2-8 from me. As our conversation on my return visit to Namgya wms more\nheated than logical, it did not become quite plain from his talk, whether he had copied\nhis paper from an old document in his possession, or from a copper-j)late of the Raja of\nBashahr. If the latter be true, this would be the first copper-plate inscription in Tibetan,,\nand the Raja of Bashahr ought to be urged to open his archives to students of history.\nThe manuscript gives a short account of the war between Ladakh and Lhasa in 1646-47\nand contains a few, but important local names. The difficulty is to assign them their’\nproper places on a map. That the document is not forged, is quite plain from its internal evidence.\n\nThe road between Namgya and Shipke is bad beyond description. I have had some\nexperience of awkward roads during my thirteen years’ residence in Indian Tibet, but\nI must say, the Namgya-Shipke road beats them all. Here we had not only to march\nby very unstable pathways along the face of the precipice, but had also from time to time’\nto climb up and down pinnacles with almost no road under our feet. It reminded me\nof chimney climbing, sometimes inside sometimes outside a chimney. The continual\nups and downs alone would have been quite sufficient to exhaust the strength of any\ntraveller on an ordinary road.\n\nThe frontier of Tibet proper is marked by a little brook, where a meal is generally\ntaken by travellers.   "passage_text": "Pindi Lai’s treasure stood us in good stead in the course of our tour, for people
continually approached us with the desire to be cured of all kinds of diseases. Government had granted us five rupees worth of Quinine and Castor Oil which had to serve as
a cure for everything. The fame of my medical skill which was, however, without any
foundation, spread far and wide. Once when travelling through the desert between
Bashahr and Spiti, and far away from any human habitation, I met with a youth and
an old woman, his mother, who said that they had travelled three days to meet me and
get medicine to cure the old woman’s eyes. As I was a Christian lama, it was my duty to
render help, they said. All who have travelled in this country know how unpleasant it
is to unload boxes in the middle of a stage, open them, and have them loaded again. In
a case like the present there was, however, no escape, and I had to get at one of my
boxes to find some ointment which would be, as I hoped, a little more efficacious than
Castor Oil. Ordinarily Pindi Lai attended to the sick who were continually hovering
about our camp and made them happy by handing over to them one or other of our blue
stones with much genial advice.

The aspect of the village of Shipke is not different from that of the villages on the
other side of the border, but the appearance of the inhabitants undoubtedly is. Not only
does their dress show the genuine Tibetan cut, but also the pigtail is much in evidence
here. I am sure that the people of Poo also were in the habit of wearing pigtails at an
earlier date than 1650 A.D. But after they had become subjects of the Bashahr Baja,
they assumed the fashions of that State. The people of Shipke try their best to extract
as much money as possible from the few European travellers, they see. But as Mr.
Schnabel said, there is some excuse, for tax-collecting is carried on in the most cruel way
all over Tibet, and they have to part with all their few rupees, when the tax-collector
comes. Only recently news was brought to Poo that an unfortunate wretch whose taxes
had not been paid for the last three years was whipped to death at Shipke. No wonder,
that most of the Tibetans would prefer to become British subjects.

There are three ruined castles at Shipke.^ The oldest of them is situated rather
high up above the village on the West. It is known by the name of mKhar-gog (broken
castle), and is built in cyclopean style (Plate XI, a). Only portions of two walls are
still in their original position. There are no traditions whatever current about this
castle. We bought an ancient stone axe of the type of the Ladakhi Kalam which was
asserted to have been found on the site of this stronghold. It is interesting that this
kind of stone implement was in use here also.

^ The earliest picture of Shipke with the Purgyul mountain is found in Seise des Srinzen TFaldemar von JPreussen
1845, Plate XXI.

E

Tlie second of the ruined castles is called Scng-gB-mKhaT (Plate XI, b). Its ruins
are found below the mKhar-gog castle, on the left bank of the Satluj. Its lower part is
built of large well fitted stones, and higher up the waUs are of clay or sun-dried bricks, as
is the case in the later Ladakhi buildings. I suppose that the castle was built by
Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal of Ladakh, and called after him. Some of the walls are still
standing. The building must have been of huge size. An inscription which I found
on a mani wall just above the village of Shipke speaks of a king and his son who once
resided ‘ at the castle.’ No names are given. The kings of Western Tibet, or their
vassal kings of Guge, may have resided here occasionally. A legend referring to this
castle, was told by the Lambardar of Shipke, and taken down by Lobzang of Poo who
accompanied me on this tour. According to it, the castle received its crooked ground
plan through a race round its base executed in opposite directions by a poisonous snake
and a scorpion.

The third castle of Shipke is situated on the road to the village of Khyug on the
brook. It is called sKyahs-mhhar ‘ castle of refuge.’ No walls are standing ; only heaps
of loose stones remain. No information of any kind regarding it was forthcoming,
and I have no idea of what age it may be.

There are long rows of may,i waUs on the road from Shipke to Khyug. The
Lambardar, Lobzang, and myself went there to examine them. The votive tablets on
them were quite of the usual style, but in the place where the Ladakhi tablets give the
name of the king, these contained the title of the Dalai Lama, and no personal name.
Por this reason it is impossible to assign a date to them or to the mani waUs. Only this
much can be said : they all date apparently from a time, not earlier than the second half
of the seventeenth century. If earlier, they would have contained names of the
kings of Ladakh, or of Guge. The tablets, however, generally contain versions of the
eulogy of the country of Guge, a kind of national anthem, and for this reason I copied
one of them, which I found in the village of Shipke. I am rather of opinion that after
1650 A.D., when Guge was made over to Lhasa, all those ancient tablets which contained the names of Ladakhi or Guge kings, were destroyed. It was in the interest of
the Lhasa Government to make people forget their former masters.

This is one of their national anthems, as we find them in these inscriptions. It is
taken from the only inscription which refers to a king.

Jambudvipa of the south is a famous country among the ten directions of the world.

There is the mountain Tise (Kailasa) with its neck of ice, the dwelling place of
those who have conquered all enemies {arhats).

There is the turquoise lake Ma-spang (Manasarovar) the abode of the Na^a
Ma-gros. “

On the right bank of the murmuring river which proceeded from an elephant’s
mouth (Satluj),

There is the great castle sKu-mkhar, the abode of the king."

  "passage_text": "CHAPTER 11.

From the Satluj to the Indus.

We left Poo on the 21st July to travel through Spiti and Eubshu to Leh. This is a
joiu’ney of about four weeks through the most uninhabitable country. Our outfit, as
regards provisions and warm clothing, might certainly have been better. But the
summers being short in these regions, we could not put in three more weeks of waiting
at Poo, to let the required goods and means come up. The missionary at Poo kindly
advanced me some money as well as tinned provisions, and we left with the determination to move on and be satisfied with the simplest fare.

On the first day we had to cross the steep Hang Pass, 16,000 feet high. It is a place
which arouses painful memories in the minds of Mr. and Mrs. Schnabel ; for when they
had to cross it the last time with a child of only two years of age, the rarified air on the
top of the pass proved to be too much for their baby which showed signs of suffocation.
Only by taking up the child and hurrying down with it at a pace not at all in harmony
with the awful condition of the road, was it possible to save its hfe. The eastern side of
the pass is very bare and uninteresting, but on the western side alpine flowers of great
beauty and scent greet the traveller, among them the wild purple aster and Aconitum
mosohatum. Before the village of Tsuling is reached on the western side, the road passes
by the ruins of the old Gadgari monastery. Heaps of loose stones and some terraced
ground is all that remains.

I could not discover anything of special interest in the little village of Tsuling, A
small hut under a huge pencil-cedar tree is called Lha-khang, “ house of the gods,” or
" temple.” It was quite empty with the exception of some drums which are kept in it.
Some stones with the inscription Om maiii padme hum were placed below the sacred
pencil -cedar.

On the 22nd July we arrived at the village of Li which looks very beautiful with its
many green fields and apricot trees in the midst of a chaos of bare rocky mountains. Li is
very probably a place with a grander past than present. The Tibetan dictionaries and chronicles speak of two ancient places called Li, one in the north, the other in the south.
The northern one has been correctly identified with Turkestan or a part of Turkestan.
Of the Li of the South it is said that it is situated “ near Nepal.” I beheve that the " Li of
the South is the Tibetan part of the present Bashahr State, the principal town of which
was very possibly the present village of Li. On a steep rock on the bank nf the river

are the ruins of an ancient castle, mkhar. People told me that they had formerly to
live on that rock (probably before 1650, ^rhen they came under Bashahr). They left the
rock on account of many accidents in consequence of their getting drunk. I visited
the site, but saw nothing beyond heaps of loose stones with fragments of rude pottery
Some of the rooms can still be traced. The Tibetans of Li as well as of Kanawar in
general are distinguished from those of Sj>iti, Ladakh and Shipke by the fashion in which
they wear their hair. The men of Kanawar wear their hair like the people of Bashahr,
Ko long pigtails are seen here. The same is the case in Lahul where also the long pigtail
has disappeared. The Hindu rulers of Bashahr and Kulu were apparently against it.

The bKra-shis-lhun-grub monastery of Li is asserted to be of ancient origin. This
may be true, for it belongs to the rNyingmapa sect, the most ancient order of monks in
Tibet. This sect has not founded new settlements for a long time. The abbot told me
that the Li monastery was founded by Padma-sambhava, which is quite probable, if it be
not even older. As Sarat Chandra Das has shown, the rNyingmapa order has much of its
literature in common with the Bonpos, the followers of the pre-Buddhist religion of
Tibet.^ Around Lhasa, the monks of the rNyingmapa order cannot be distinguished from
other orders of the “ red persuasion, ” as regards dress, but here in the west they can.

Here the rNying-ma-pa monks grow long
hair which is never combed, and gives them a
savage appearance. The best specimens of this
uncivilized order of saints can, however, be
seen at Pyin in Spiti. Although I am convinced of the correctness of the assertion that
the monastery is of remote origin, this statement cannot be confirmed by documentary
evidence. The present building does not
appear to be of many yeans’ standing, nor the
few idols contained in it. At the monastery,
however, they have an ancient and beautiful
wood carving of teak wood, representing Buddha
surrounded by Bodhisattvas. All the Bodhisattvas are of the primitive and simple type.

(Kg. 1).

Not far from the bKra-shis-lhun-grub monastery, a little above the line of cultivation, are
the ruins of an old nunnery, called Jo-moi
dgon-pa. It consists of three separate ruined
houses, a mani wall covered with white pebbles
and two mchod-rten. The nunnery was abandoned only a hundred years ago, so people told me,

The irrigation canals of Li are of some interest. In one case the water is conducted through a rock or mountain by a tunnel of considerable length. People here'
firmly believe that this tunnel was made by fairies {mkha-’agro) or gods (lha). In the-
West people would be proud of their clever ancestors.

In one of the mcTiod-rten at Li, on the road to Nako, I found a clay tablet representing Avalokite^vara with eleven heads and eight arms, an interesting stage in this
divinity’s development into a figure with a thousand arms."

It is called Lha-brang and\nbelongs to the Gelugpa order. Although I was assiued that it contained ancient pictures,\nI could not manage to visit it. iN'or did I see the ancient stone sculpture at Kyahar\nwhich is said to be similar to the Avalokite4vara of Chang, mentioned above.\n\nOn a rook below the joresent village of Kyahar are extensive ruins of a deserted\nvillage. The jBxst march\ntook us to the Zangzam bridge, which spans a tributary of the Spiti river. Here the\nroad leads through Tibetan territory for several miles, and the camp on the bridge as well\nas our next camp at Horling was on Tibetan ground. Strange to say, we passed by mmi walls, from\ntime to time, and several of the stones placed on, or by the side of, the walls, were of unusual interest. They contained the names. of the great reformer Tsong-kha-pa and three of his\ncontemporaries, _ mKhas-grub-pa (1384-1437), Lha-dbang-blo-gros (1388-1462), and\n\np 2\n\ndGe’adun-grab (1389’1473). They could not believe that a ‘ king ’\nshould ever have resided at the now unimportant village of Tsaparang. But d’Andrada\nis vindicated as we know now that Tsaparang was the capital of a sovereign whose power\nwas acknowledged even as far as Spiti. As far as my knowledge goes, the kingdom of Guge has had three\ncapitals : the first was mTho-lding (Tholing), the second, Tsaparang, the third Garthog.\nThe genealogical tree of the kings of Guge has been preserved in Tibetan historical works.\nThe original line of these kings came from Zangskar, as stated above. Their dynastical\nname was Lde. The Lde dynasty came to an end in the principal line, and was superseded by a rMal dynasty. When the rMal dynasty became extinct, a member of a side\nbranch of the original Lde dynasty was invited from Purang and became king of Guge.\nThen the historical information ceases. The name of the king who is mentioned on\nthe votive tablet, is Khri-bkra-shis-grags-pa-lde. It is, therefore, very probable that Khri-bkra-shis-grags-pa-lde is\nthe very king whose acquaintance was made by d’Andrada in 1623 A.D.\n\nThis supposition is strengthened by the discovery of a similar votive tablet which I\nmade three days after at Tabo in Spiti. This contained the name of the same king and\ngave Tsaparang as his residence. But what is still more surprising, is the occurrence of\nthe following short passage on the same tablet : “ He who clears away all the apostacy and\ndarkness at the great palace of Tsaiarang rise’’ The man who carved this inscription\nwas evidently displeased with the Tsaparang king’s inclination towards Christianity.\nSo was the king of Leh; for it was probably on this account that he placed his\nyounger brother on the throne of Guge. that of the Tabo monastery. This shoe's that in the 15th century people belieyed in
a connection between the Tabo monastery of Spiti, and the great priest-kings of
Guge.

From Horling, the high and beautiful snow mountains near the Tillage of Chang,
which belong to the group of the Purgyul peaks and are over 22,000 feet high, can be
seen. W e had already admired them on our way to Shipke, when we were much closer to
them (Plate X, a). At Namgya, I had heard the following ditty about them : —

Tise gangsTiyi rgyalpo yin
Vurgyul rii rgyalpo yin
Maspang mifisoyi rgyalpo yin.

“ Kailasa is the king of glaciers,

Purgyul is the king of mountains,

Manasarowar is the king of lakes.”

At Hoiiing the coolies from Chang, pointing towards the Purgyul group of mountains which is here called Gung-ri (perhaps the Ktingrang of the maps), said that on those
mountains was the fabulous ’aBa-yul, the abode of spirits. Its inhabitants are believed to
be numerous, but ordinary people can neither see nor hear them. It is only very good
men or lamas who are capable of perceiving anything. When such a pious man approaches that region of eternal snow, he hears the voices of its invisible denizens or the
barking of their ghostly dogs, but sees nothing. This tale reminds me strongly of a
passage which I had repeatedly found in inscriptions with reference to the Kailasa
mountains : — dgra hcom bzJiugs gnas Tise, ‘ Kailasa, the abode of those who have conquered all enemies’ {arhats). The ice mountains evidently are not only the abode of the
gods, but also that of the dead who, according to the belief of the Tibetans, have
acquired paradise.

We reached Lhari, the first village of Spiti, on the 28th July. Although this village
is possibly connected with the history of gNya-khri-btsam-po, the first king of Tibet, it is
nowadays a very poor place. It consists of only a few scattered houses. Above it, on
the side next the brook, there are the extensive ruins of an ancient castle, called Serlang,
the former abode of the Lhari people. Below the village there are very many ancient
rock-carvings, among which we note, in particular, the ibex and the svastika. One of the
carvings appears to represent the ‘ willow of the world ’ with its six branches and six
roots, one of the symbols of the pre-Buddhist religion of the people. Another symbol
appears to represent the sun and the moon. Dilapidated as Lhari is now-a-days, I cannot
escape the impression that it is a very ancient settlement.

On the 29th July, we marched to the famous Gelugpa monastery of Tabo which is
only three miles distant from Lhari (Plate XIV, a). When we were approaching it, I

said to Pindi Lai : “ You see, popular tradition connects this monastery witli Ein-clienbzang-po who lived 900 years ago, and an inscription at Holding showed us that such
traditions were also current in the 16th century. But what is the use of all these traditions ? We must have literary proof that a monastery actually goes hack to those early
days; if possible, we must have a document of those very times, on which it is plainly
stated that the erection of the monastery actually took place at that time. I wonder if
ever we shall be able to prove any such assumption!” As I said this, I little thought
that a few hours after, I should have ample proof in hand.

In the vicinity of the Tabo monastery are many rows of 108 small mchocl-rten, but
one of them numbered at least 216 (Plate XIV, b). They were the forerunners of the
mani walls in Western Tibet. Besides these rows, there are many ruined mchod-rten
round about, and countless rock carvings. The latter represent mostly the iljex and the
smstiha and are possibly of pre-Buddhist origin. On the hill side, almost like cave
dwellings, are the winter houses of the lamas.

The temple buildings are found on the plain above the river. They are surrounded
by a high mud wall. I made a plan of the whole establishment and these are some ot‘ the
measurements taken. Extreme length : 313 feet, 7 inches ; breadth 257 feet 3 inches.
Within this enclosure exist seven temple-halls, and a great number of mchod-rten. The
monks took me from one temple to another without showing me the principal hall. They
said that only a Commissioner (the highest personage they have ever heard of) could l)e
permitted to enter there. I tried in vain to convince them that, with regard to their
treasures, I was in as high an office as a Commissioner, until I produced two rupees.
Then the doors to their holy of holies were thrown open, and I presume that nothing of
interest was purposely concealed from us.

The principal hall is called rNam-par-snang-mdzad. The length of this hall with
additional apse is 63 feet, 14 inches and its breadth 34 feet, 10 inches. The principal
image is a white stucco statuette of rNam-par-snang-mdzad (Vairochana) consisting of four complete figures seated back to back (Plate XV, a). Along the walls, 6 or 7
feet above the ground, there are thirty-two raised medallions with exceedingly well executed stucco figures of life size (Plates XV, b ; XVI and XVII, b). Nobody in the monastery
at present knows whom they represent. But I am inclined to believe that they represent
the thirty-three Hindu gods.^ The figure of Ganela, which would make up the full
number, seems to have lost its original position above the door. It is now found on the
altar, below rNam-par-snang-mdzad (Plate XVII, a). One of the figures by the side
of the door was recently furnished with a new head like a modern Lamaist dancing
mask, the old head having been.lost (Plate XVII, b)."
}

Most of the pictures refer to the story of Buddha’s life, beginning with the descent of the
white elephant from heaven. On both sides of the door were painted the four Lokapalas,
as we find them so often. On the right and left wall there was the medicine Buddha
with his followers, Sakya thub-pa, B.in-ehen-zla-ba ; Myang-ngan-med-mchog-dpal ; Ohosgrags-rgya-mthsoi-dpal ; gSer-bzang-dri-med ; mNgon-mkhyen-rgyal-po and mThsan-legs.
Most of the pictures in this hall were furnished with explanatory inscriptions in modern
Tibetan. Like all the remaining halls, it had apparently been renovated in a sweeping
way. All the ancient frescoes and inscriptions had been scratched off, and new pictures
painted on the old walls.

G

When we were at- Tabo, we met a native painter, who was prepared to renovate
everything. The monks of the monastery had been told that Government would undertake to pay for necessary repairs in their temples and had asked the Assistant Commis-
sioner to let them have the services of an artist. Accordingly, Mr. Howell, I.C.S., had
ordered a painter to go to Tabo and apply his art to its ancient walls, fortunately, he
had not yet started work in the principal hall, but in all the other halls, there remained
little which had not been destroyed either by him or by previous artists. I told the man
that he was on no account to touch the walls of the central hall, and when I met Mr.
Howell about a week later in Spiti, he promised to give strict orders that no further
attempt should be made to “improve ” this precious relic of the past.

The gSer-gyi-lha-khang is another picture hall to the left of the preceding one
AH the pictures in it are modern, and it has an inscription Oni mani padme hum in
.LaMhsa characters running round the four walls,

The dKyii-khang is a picture hall behind the preceding. As the roof is not ■watertight, the pictures have suffered much through leakage. The principal picture shows
rNam-par-snang-mdzad, but I could discover no inscriptions in it.

In Lha-khang-dkar-byung, a pictme hall behind the preceding, the central picture
shows Buddha with two disciples ; to the left of this group wo see Tsong-kha-pa. The
other pictures in this hall can no more be explained. There were no inscri])tions.

The picture hall Brom-ston was evidently named after tlic famous pupil of Atlsa,
called by that name, the founder of the bKa-gdams-pa sect. It is situated on the right
hand side of the Central Hall. It was probably erected in Brom-ston’s time, but nothing
remains of ancient relics, besides the interesting door of thamj -shiny (Deodar wood)
which is decorated with well executed carvings of Buddhist saints. The stylo of carving
is very different from the present Tibetan style, and is a distiuguishi.ng characteristic of
the half Indian Buddhism of the 11th century. This hall is without inscriptions and the
principal picture in it represents Buddha with his two disciples.

The seventh hall called Byams-pa-chen-moi-lha-khang contains a huge stucco statue
of Maitreya seated on a chair. The top of his head may be 18 to 20 feet above the
ground. This hall contains pictures of Tibetan architecture, perhaps four to five centuries
ago, such as the monastery of Tashilumpo (bKra-shis-lhun-po) and the Potala palace of
Lhasa. But most of the other pictm’es in this hall are modern restorations or inventions.
Here I noticed a Wartu inscription, probably an Ommani padme hum formula. This
haU has also a door carved with Buddhist figures in Indian, not Tibetan style. The
central figure on the lintel, however, is Gane^a.

Besides these seven principal halls, I must also mention the entrance haU to the principal temple, Lha-khang-chen-moi-sgo-khang. It is furnished with paintings, for
instance Tsong-kha-pa with two disciples, one of whom was called mKhas-grub.

The thick darkness of most of the Tibetan temples is a great hindrance to archaeological research. My work had to be done in a different way from that done at Pompei or
in the^ Turkestan deserts. At Pompei and in Turkestan every article which comes to
light, is valuable and has to be taken up, labelled, and put aside. In an inhabited place

Plate XIX.

b. Rope bridge near Lithang.

like Tabo, I bad, bowerer, to select among bundreds of inscrijjtions and objects of art,
tliose wbicb were of real value for tbe study of Tibetan bistory and art, tvbicb meant a
close examination of many objects and records in a badly lighted 25 lace. When, finally,
tbe most interesting bad been decided upon, tbe second part of our work, pbotograjjhy, and
copying in writing as well as in colours, began. Considering tbe very great difficulties
be bad to encounter, I must say that Piudi Lai achieved wonders with Ms camera. But
tbe bttle light that entered this ball through a minute bole in tbe ceiling was not sufficient for tbe lamas, whom I set to work on tbe j)aintings and wall inscriptions. Then
we thought of our small supjfiy of candles and by giving three of them to our helpmates,
we made three Tibetan hearts happier than they bad ever been. I^one of them bad
apparently ever possessed a candle, and now think of the grand sport they bad,
working in a dark corner of the temple with a real European candle by their side, h’o
Maharaja could have taken greater pride in the electric light newly introduced into his
capital.

Within the walled enclosure about the temples, there are many mchod-rten, and
several of them have frescoes inside. There is also a botanical ciuiosity in tMs court ; for
here we find the only apricot trees existing in the barren and cold country of Spiti wbicb
is separated by a girdle of deserts from all the neighbouring territories of Tibet, Ladakh,

The monastery is built in three stories, the one\nabove always a little narrower than the one below it, like a pyramid of three steps,\nthus reminding me of the Alchi (and also of the mTho-lding) monastery. Natbang also\nis said to have been founded in the days, when the Tabo monastery was built. During\nsummer, there is not a single lama residing in it.\n\nIn the village of Phog, I met with Mr. OargiU of the Pubbc Works Department,\nwho was on tour through these outlying districts examining the bridges. He invited me\nto dinner, and I spent a very pleasant evening with Mm.\n\nOn the 31st July, we arrived at Drangkhar called Bravg-niMar or Grang-mkhar in\ninscriptions (Plate XIX, a). The monastery of this town, the capital of Spiti, is called\nIdha-od-pai-dgon-pa^ Lha-od seems to be tbe local pronunciation of Zla-od, the name of\na famous lama who was born in 1121, according to the Eeu-mig. Zla-’od-pa would then\nmean “a follower of Zla-’od.” He is apparently the founder or renovator of the\nmonastery which now belongs to the Gelugpa order. The monks assert that it was not\nonly of earlier origin than the Tabo monastery, but also earlier than tbe times of\nSrong-btsan-sgam-po. They have, however, nothing to show of really ancient relics.\nThey explain tMs fact by stating that the monastery was plundered many times, lastly\nduring the Pogra war, which is in agreement with my History of Western Tibet. Traces\nof the ravages of that war may be plainly seen in aU the monasteries of Spiti wMch we\n\ne 2\n\nTisited on our journey, with the exception of Tabo. Why did Tabo alone escape\ndestruction ? I am inclined to believe that Tabo was under Bashahr in those times,\nand that the Dogras did not wish to interfere with the government of that state.\nWe found three, probably modern, stucco statues in the central hall. They represent\nByams-pa (Maitreya), seated crosslegged, with a kind of tea-pot in his hand ; Buddha ;\nand the lama Chos-drag, a contemporary of Srong-btsan-sgam-po. The statue of Chos-drag\nlooks like the illustration of the same personage in Griinwedel’s Mythology.\n\nThere are frescoes on the walls of this temple, but now only very little of them can\nbe made out. The following figures could be distinguished : ’Od-dpag-med (Amitabha) ;\nPadma-sambhava ; and dGe-bai-bshes-gnyeu (Kalyana-mitra).\n\nAbove one of the doors there is an inscription in modern characters and orthograj)hy\nwhich, I was told, contained the name of dGe-bai-bshes-gnyen. It is called Lha-bla-mai-dgon-pa, and thus by its name it\ndirectly -points to tbe great priest- king of Guge, Lba-bla-ma-ye-shes-’od, whoso name\nwe had found in an inscription at Poo. Local tradition says that King Lha-bla-ma or, as.\nanother man understood it, the gods {Iha) and the lamas {blama) built it in one night.\n\nAt Lhanartsa I spent two enjoyable and instructive days with the A^istant Commissioner. Here I had an attack of malarial fever, and Mr\" Howell did everything in\n\n* Mistory of Western Tibet, p, 163 .\n\niPSi:\n\nMs ] 30 wer to cure me and make me fit for the road. Mr. Howell Avas just engaged in revising the Spiti portion of the Kangra Gazetteer, and as he had the Nono of Spiti as well\nas lamas of various denominations encamped in the vicinity, our time was sjAentin a very\nprofitable way. Let me briefly review the principal points of our enquiries about Spiti.\n\nThere are now-a-days five principal monasteries in Spiti, which represent three sects of\nLamaism. The Tabo, Drangkhar, and Ki monasteries belong now to the Ge-lug-pa sect.\nThe Kaze monastery belongs to the Sa-skya-pa sect, and the Pyin monastery belongs to\nthe rNying-ma-pa. Whilst the four first mentioned monasteries do not differ essentially from Central Tibetan establishments, Avith Avhich they keep up intercourse, the\nPyin monastery has no connection Arith Lhasa, and maintains those traditions which\nhave been handed down from the times of the most primitive Lamaism. I have already\nmentioned the wild appearance of its monks, and as Mr. Lyall tells us in the Gazetteer\nthese monks were blamed for their uncivilised condition by a Lhasa emissary who travelled\nthrough Spiti. This observation is of great interest\nfor this kind of head-dress seems to have been handed down in Spiti from the earliest time\nof Tibetan Buddhism. We read in the Tarlung part of the rGyal-rabs that king Ealpacan had silken streamers tied to his looks, and that he was connected by such streamers\nwith the lamas who surrounded him The close connection of the rNying-ma<pa form\nof Lamaism AAith the pre-Buddhist Bon religion has already been noticed, and the Pyin\nmonastery of Spiti seems to be a particularly favourable place to study it. I still regret\nthat our limited time did not allow us to visit it. One of those Bu-rzhan lamas was in\nMr. Howell’s camp, and gave us much information. Unfortunately, his dialect was so\nunusual, that I could not make out all he said. The escort carried\nsmall flags and twenty white satin umbrellas. The band consisted of musical reeds, bagpipes, guitars, and other instruments. With sonorous and grave music, and uttering the\nsacred mantra, Om matii padme hum, they approached the holy sage to offer him a\nrespectful welcome in the name of the king of Guge. *\n\n^ THe eight great places o£ pilgrimage (Sanskrit mahasthana) aie 1st the Lninbini Garden (modem Eummindei in the Nepal\nTarai) where Buddha was born ; 2iii Bodh Gaya where he attained enlightenment ; 3rd the Deei’park (modern Samath) near\nBenares where he preached his first sermon ; 4th Kusinara (modern Kasia ?) where he reached Nirvana ; 5th th Jetarana\nnear Sravasti (modern Saheth-Maheth), where the great miracle took place, 6th Yaisaii (modem BasSrh) where he was fed by\na monkey ; 7th Samkasya (modem Sankisa) where he descended from heaven, and 8th Bajagriha (modern Eajgii‘) where he\nsubdued the wild elephant. We do not know that the tea plant is eaten, but\nthe leaves are churned in warm water, and the soup is drunk. It has many properties ! ” Thereupon Ati^a, who could pay compliments like any French abb6, remarked :\n“ So excellent a beverage as tea must have originated from the moral merits of the monks\nuf Tibet!”\n\nThe Manasarowar Lake pleased Ati4a so much that he stayed there for seven days.\nThen he proceeded to mTho-lding, the capital of Guge, where he was received by the\nking with due honours. Although all the lamas and noblemen rose respectfully when\nAti^a approached them, the old lama, Ein-chen-bzang-po, would not rise, partly from\n■envy, partly from weakness. But then Ati4a displayed his intellectual armour in\nsuch a brilliant way before the old monk that even he was conquered and ready to sit\nat the feet of the newcomer.^ After a residence in Guge of two years, Ati^a proceeded\n^to Central Tibet. He died at Nyethang near Lhasa at the age of seventy-three in the\nyear 1053 A.D. The founding of the so-called half-reformed sects of Lamaism was\ndue to his exertions. The most important of them is the bKa-gdams-pa sect. It was\nin monasteries of this sect that Tsong-kha-pa studied, before he started the great reform\nmovement which ended in the creation of the Ge-lug-pa sect. The object of all these\nreformations was not, as is often supposed, to go back to the early Buddhism as it was\npreached by Gautama, but to build up a church which represented the doctrines of the\nMahayana school of Buddhism in a pure form. The doctrines of N agarjuna were propounded by all the great teachers of Tibet. But the Kala-chakra philosophy with its\nmonotheistic tendencies was also favoured by them.\n\nOn the 10th August, we travelled to the southern end of the lake, and then along\nIts western shore, and at sunset we arrived at bKor-rdzod (map Karzok. Plate XXIII).\nThe sudden appearance of the monastery in that barren desert was such a surprise that\nit was at first difficult to believe in its reality. On this march, the Tibetan fauna was\nmuch in evidence. There wore large herds of rhyang (wild asses which look like mules),\nand one of the rhyang came quite close to us and watched our caravan passing by.\nThere were very many hares and marmots which did not show any signs of fear, and\nalso the beautiful tail-less rats of Tibet looked at us curiously from behind many a stone.\nWhilst animal life was thus well represented on dry land, I could not discover any\nliving being in the water of the lake. But as aquatic plants were plentiful it attracted\n-wild geese and ducks, of which we saw a good number. As Drew says, gulls have their\nbreeding ground on an island in the lake. In spite of the desolation round about,\nthe scenery is very fine. Cunningham gives\nthe legend of the lake which explains its unusual name. W e heard the same legend at\nbKor-rdzod. Although the tale is quite without a point, Cunningham says that it is as\ngood as many a Greek tale. The word Thsomo means ‘lake,’ and iJw’i is an ex-\n■clamation used by people when driving yaks. According to the tale, an old woman\n■ came riding on a yak and made the animal wade into the water. She was shouting Min\nall the time, and was finally drowned together with her yak. It is strange that Trebeck\ndoes not make any mention of a monastery on the lake, although he travelled along its\nwestern shore. All the same, the convent must have been in existence in his time, for in\nan inscription which I found on one of the many mani walls which line the lake shore,\nthe expression dGon-snying, ancient monastery, was used with reference to it. These\nma'^i walls extend to about two miles in both directions from the monastery (Plate\nXXIV, a) . The votive tablets on these walls contained the names of several chiefs of the\nPubshu nomads who have their residence close to the monastery. Of royal Ladakhi\nnames, I found only two mentioned, those of the two last independent rulers of Ladakh.\nBut another tablet near the monastery contained a very beautiful hymn on Tibet, especially\nits western parts. This hymn was more of a geographical than historical character.\nW e took an impression of this inscription, and I had to make an eye-copy in addition.\n\nI visited the monastery next morning and was disappointed to hear that it was a\nmodern structure, between fifty and sixty years old.^ The old monastery stood on the\nbrook, below the present site ; but not a trace of it now remains. The few ancient\nimages and other articles of worship were taken up to the present building. Among\nthe antiquities pointed out to us, were several miniature mchod-rien of the usual type.\n• Of all the stucco figures, and of a fine wood-carving in sandal wood, which represented\nPadma-sambhava with two of his fairy friends, it was asserted that fifty or sixty years ago\nthey had been brought up here from gSham, Lower Ladakh. I suspect that these Eubshu\npeople bought up the entire contents of a ruined monastery in Lower Ladakh. The principal stucco figure represents Buddha with two disciples, and another Padma-sambhava.\nThe names of the other images, I did not try to ascertain, because the history of their\ndate and origin will always remain obscure. I may mention here, that outside, near the\nsite of the ancient monastery, I found a relievo representing Padma-sambhava, carved\non a beautiful slab of snow-white quartz. I was greatly tempted to carry it off, but it\nwould have been too heavy. One of the clay pots in the bKor-rdzod monastery reminded\n,me of the stone age of Europe. It had evidently been made by plastering the inside of\na basket with clay and then burning the basket. All the books at this monastery were\nmodern Tibetan prints.\n\nThe neck ornament of a man at bKor-rdzod who acted as Lambardar, attracted my\nA attention, because it was of cruciform shape, and could at first sight be taken for a\nChristian ornament. He said, he had excavated it from a high hiU in the neighbourhood.\n\n^ A picture of the old monastery is found in Schlagintweits* B&isen in Indien und Soohasien Jena 1872-18.\n\nI bought it from him for two rupees. It was made of a mixture of metals, similar tO'\nthe Indian kliansl. It was a plain cross with beams of equal length, and at the end of\neach beam was found a double spiral as an ornament. As I was told by another man\nfrom Eubshu, there are ruins of ancient settlements and watercourses all over the\ncountry. They are found on high bill s in Eubshu, and are ascribed to a tribe of Mon,\nthe pre-Tibetan inhabitants of the country. These Mon must have been marvels of\nendurance. How they could have cultivated fields at those altitudes, is a mystery. The\nbarley fields of the bKor-rdzod monastery are in Mr. Drew’s opinion the highest in the\nworld (Plate XXII, b). But those of the Mon settlers must have been higher still.\nAccording to Survey maps,^ the altitude of bKor-rdzod is 16,600 feet, but according to\nDrew it is only 15,000 feet high. Drew gives the following numbers with regard to this\nlake : length 16 miles, breadth 3 to 5 miles ; depth 248 feet. It may sound incredible\nthat there should have been fields still higher than the present fields of bKor-rdzod whose\nharvest sometimes fails. But I remember that also on one of my former journeys, in\nZangskar, I came across the ruins of a Dard settlement at an altitude where it was icy\ncold even in summer."

As tho cx-king was married to his\nown sister, this picture represented some of his nearest relation, and he implored mo\nnot to go away without making him a present of it. There remained no alternative\nfor me but to tear the picture out of the book, and hand it over to him. It was\nhowever, fortunate for us, to have placed under obligation sucli an important personage through this little present. Por, if we had not been in his favour, it would\nprobably have taken a long time before the nomads found yaks for us. As matters\nstood, the yaks turned up in good condition next morning. In the same way, it was\nalso our good fortune to have met with the Assistant Commissioner in Spiti. Otherwise\nwe should certainly have had diflGLculty in getting transport animals from Spiti to the\nlake. It must be remembered that animals as well as men are scarce in tlicse frontier\nregions, that the roads are dMcult, if not dangerous, and that these frontier people\ncan hardly be reached by any authority. Last year, as Mr. Ho^vell told me, transport\nwas absolutely refused to a traveller in Spiti, who obtained it only by using desperate\nmeans.\n\nAs we have been travelling on yaks for some time, and as we have before us many\nmore miles of yak riding, it seems the proper place to say a few words about these interesting Tibetan animals. The first yak ride we had on our way hack from Shipke,\nand the second on the journey from Spiti to the lake. All those yaks had rings through\ntheir noses, and could in a way be controlled by them, for it requires great anger on tho\npart of the yak to make him indifferent to the pain which would be caused by his tearing himself free and running away. But the yaks which we received for our journey\n\n^ Surrey Map of 1874. Sheet 46 gives Karzofc as 14,960 ft. [Ed.]\n\nPlate XXV.\n\na. Nomads’ camp on Lake Thsomo Riri.\n\nb. Yaks on the shore of Lake Thsomo Riri.\n\nfrom bKor-rclzod to Nyoma on the Indus, and from Nyoma to rGya in Ladakh, 'vrere\nwithout this last touch of culture, a nose-ring. They had neither saddles, nor bridles,\nnor even nose-rings, they were absolutely undefiled products of nature. When I asked the\nnomads why even this last remnant of civilisation was not found on them, they said that\nthis particular breed of yaks did not possess any noses. I was pitying the poor creatures\nfor whom the roses had no scent, when I noticed that two little holes could he distinguished above the mouth. That in these circumstances it was no easy matter to use the\nyaks for riding, can well he imagined. In fact, their management was so difficult, that\nI would have gladly renounced this doubtful pleasure altogether, if the ratified air of\nthose altitudes had not compelled me to use these uninviting beasts. When I was tired, I\nwould tell one of the nomads to get me a yak for riding. Then all the men would run in\nfront of the herd of yaks they were driving, shouting at them and waving their arms in the\nair, to make them understand that they were wanted to stop. A single one could never\nbe made either to stop or to start. Their esprit de corps was so strong that they insisted\non doing everything together. Now, when the herd was stopped, one of the unladen yaks\nwas singled out for my use and seized by the horns. Naturally he disliked this treatment,\nand whilst he was dancing round the man, I was supposed to fly through the air and\n'drop on the yak’s back. As soon as I had reached my seat and seized its mane, the\nnomad would let go the horns, and off went the yak galloping up and down the hillside,\nuntil he had found his natural equilibrium, when he joined the herd again. The nomads\nhad the kindness to select for me the least savage of their yaks, but the Khalasi and\nKhansaman had to take what remained, and that led often to exciting performances.\nI still see the Khalasi seated on the tail and hindquarters (for he had failed to drop\ndown in the middle part of the animal) of a furious yak, which charged up and down\nwith him on very uneven ground on the Thaglang Pass. Then, when the yak had found\nhis place in the caravan of snorting beasts, he would look out for another yak, his adversary, and poke him with his horns. The opponent, naturally offended by this act of\nspecial attention, would pay it back in the same coin. In these continual fights, the\nyaks knocked a lock off one of our boxes, made holes in several others, and smashed the\ntripod of our camera. That they did not smash our own legs, was due to the continual\ncare with which we watched these fights. Whenever one’s own yak was charged by his\nadversary, one had to lift high the threatened leg, and join in the struggle by using one’s\nstick and umbrella. There was, however, one weapon which was respected by all the\nyaks. That wns the stone whip of Eubshu. We were now in the centre of a large treeless country, and thus it is not to be wondered at, that even the whip should be a stone\nimplement. It was an oblong stone, three to four pounds in weight, with which the\nyaks were hammered on their hind quarters, whenever they showed signs of laziness.\nCuriously, the a.TiiTna.1s seemed to fear the sight of this stone implement more than its\nweight. The one I was riding on was often energetically hammered by a nomad behind\nme, a treatment which he endured with the utmost indifference. But the moment he saw\nanother nomad using his stone against a yak in front of him, he shuddered with terror.\nWhen the hammering failed to make an impression, the stones were thrown at the yaks.\n\nOnce, tlie Khalasi had such a stone flung at his leg, which caused him to complain\nbitterly, as he was an official personage, hut the nomads explained that it was intended\nfor the yak."

Its depth is 67 feet\naccording to Drew. Its water is brackish, like that of the Thsomo Diri. There is no\npermanent habitation on its shore, but many stone walls have been erected by the\nnomads who often have their encampment on this lake. The scenery round about is\nvery grand and of the same character as on the Thsomo E.iri.\n\nOn the 13th August, we had our camp near Raldrong, where the Phuga brook enters\nthe Indus. Opposite the confluence are the ruins of a Mon village. This is probably\nthe deserted village mentioned by the late Dr. Shawe in his letter of the 19th J uly 1900,\nin which he advised me to visit Nyoma and surroundings. Dr. Shawe wrote as follows:\n“ Some miles west of Nyoma are said to be the remains of an old Mon village, where I was\ntold boxes, household utensils, and coins have been found (apparently in graves). Unfortunately I did not hear of this till I had left and was across the Indus, or I would\nhave made enquiries. Coins should prove interesting and instructive,” From the left\nbank of the Indus we could see deserted fields in terraces, a group of houses, and walls.\nAs, however, the distance from Nyoma was fully ten miles, and we were perfectly ex--\nhausted from our long desert journey, I could not manage to visit the site. In Nyoma\nI tried to obtain some of the articles found by the people at this deserted village, but\nthey pretended not to possess any such things.\n\nOn the 14!th August, we marched to Nyoma, where we had our camj) on the loft bank\nof the Indus. Pindi Lai and myself crossed the Indus on a little raft of inflated skins.\nThe river journey on this raft, where four men had to sit motionless on a single square\nyard, occupied fuUy half an hour. Pindi Lai got a slight touch of the sun, and a\nsevere headache prevented him from enjoying the shade of the first willows after Kaze\nin Spiti, to which he had been looking forward. He was, however, bravo enough to take\nsome photos of objects of interest.\n\nThe elevation of Nyoma (Nimu, Nima, etc., on maps) is given as about 14,000 feet\nby Drew. This is certainly exaggerated. It could hardly be more than 13,000. Dro\"W\nmentions the few large wfllow trees of great age at the village. They would not be\nfound, we may be sure, at an elevation of 14,000. Besides, we saw very many young\nand thriving ones. Before speaking of our own experiences, let me quote Dr. Shawe’s\nobservations according to his letter of the 19th July 1906. He says : “ Here (at\nNyoma) are very fine remains of a castle and old town on the top of a rock (Plate XXVI, a)..\nThe buildings all more or less destroyed except the temple which is said to be of the\nsame date as the rest, and contains a fine lot of small brass idols and other temple\nutensils. The town is said to have been built by bDe-skyong-mam-rgyal (c. 1730 A.D.)\nwhose name I also found on a man,i wall. The only other king’s name was Don-grub -\nrnam-rgyal (1790 1841), but there are many old maijA walls, both of the ordinary and of\nthe shelf type. On the plain behind the rock are extensive remains of a village whiclt\n\ntlie. jjeople said, was of the same date as the castle, but which appeared to me much older\nfrom the style of building, also two or three \" step mchod-rten'\" but no ladder in the\nmiddle of sides (like those of. the AlcM-mhhar-gog carvings). One old mchod-rten of the\nordinary type, now fast falling to pieces, had a small door at either end, some three feet\nhigh, and the interior was very finely decorated with paintings of Buddha’s temptation,\nhis subduing demons, etc. The decorations of the ceiling were in relievo. It is by far\nthe finest piece of vnchod~rten decoration I have seen yet. The only rock carving I\ncould find was a migmang (kind of chessboard) on a boulder, but no inscriptions on\nrocks at all.”\n\nAs we see, Dr. Shawe himself did not feel satisfied with the people’s statement that\nthe town of Nyoma was built by bDe-skyong-rnam-rgyal. He found distinct signs of\nan earlier origin. The old types of mchod-rten especially, and the fact that one of them\nwas beautifully decorated inside, point to an age of at least 900 to 1,000 years. I went\nto examine the temple which occupies the highest position in the now deserted town\non the rook and belongs to the ’aBrug-pa order of monks. Since Dr. Shawe had been\ntold that the temple was built in the 18th centruy, the monks had altered their opinion,\nand I was told that it dated from the days of King Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal (c. 1600). I was,\nhowever, not satisfied with an assertion which possibly had no real foundation and\nasked the monks to show me proof of this assertion. Then they brought me a book\nwhich had been dedicated to the monastery by Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal and actually contained\na dedication sheet on which the names of the king and his illustrious queen bSkal-bzang\ncould be distinctly read. Of course, a document like that goes to prove only that Senga\nge-rnam-rgyal took a certain interest in the settlement, and possibly renovated the\ntemple. It is difficult to believe that there was nothing before Seng-ge-rnam-rgyaTs\ndays in a pleasant vaUey like Nyoma, and ancient mchod-rten distinctly point to a time,\nearlier than this king. One of the many painted flags {thang-ka) in this temple, particularly interested me, for it not only contained an idealised portrait of Seng-ge-rnam-\nrgyal’s friend, the great lama sTag-thsang-ras-pa, but also scenes of the royal household\n300 years ago. I wanted by all means to have it photographed, and as Pindi Lai was\nnot well enough to climb up to this temple above the present town, I asked permission\nto take the picture down to the bungalow. This request was not granted, until I had\ninterviewed a high lama of Hemis who was touring in the district."
}
