  "passage_text": "On this picture we see a number of whitewashed houses, one or two stories high.\nThey look exactly like the present Ladakhi houses and also have a red or black band\nround the roof, just as the present monasteries have. Then we see the inside of the\nroyal kitchen with five or six people busy at work, and the male and female members of\nthe royal family in separate rooms. Below the houses are painted two processions which\napproach the buildings from right and left. The men on the right hand side are riding\non mules or rkyangs, and those on the left are walking, carrying presents, perhaps tribute.\nThe. chief value of the picture lies in the fact that the costumes of those times ar(i painted\nso well. Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal is the king who is credited by popular tradition with the\nintroduction of the Ladakhi type, of dress, as it remained unchanged down to the time\n\nI\n\nof the Pogra war. In a collection of Tibetan proverbs which I acquired from a man from\nrGya some years ago, and which is among the manuscripts brought to Simla, there is\na proverb which refers to the change of dress under this king. There it is stated that\nthe king, whose name S6nQ~y€ means “ lion,** said that he was willing to honoui his\nsubjects by giving them one of his ears ; thus the men received the high black cap,\ncalled s6ng-g6 Ttioi-wbchog, “ lion’s ear ” which I finci pictured by Drew. The same proverb informs us that the great tiger lama {sTag means a tiger) favoured the women by\ngiving them his spotted skin. Thus the dark blue dress of the Ladakhi women with its\nred and yellow spots was introduced. The picture in the Nyoma monastery does not,\nhowever, show the new fashion, having possibly been painted before its introduction.\nAll the male persons wear turbans, as was the fashion in Western Tibet from c. 1000\nA.D. downwards. The royal ladies are distinguished by their rich herags, fillets\nof leather which are covered with precious stones. Although I have not yet been able\nto trace them on pictures earlier than c. 1530 A.D., I am convinced that this fashion\ngoes back to examples of old Indian art, where the Nagas and Nagis were represented\nby a human figure with a snake growing out of the back and over-topping their heads.\nThe herag of the Ladakhi women which begins in the middle of the back and becomes\nbroader over the head, looks like the representation of a snake. Perhaps the Ladaklii\nwomen wished to look like Nagis, because these water fairies were famous for their\nbeauty.\n\nWe spent Sunday, the 15th August, on the left bank of the Indus river, opposite\nNyoma, and resumed our journey on Monday the 16th. Our next aim was Leh, and as\nthe road along the Indus river was impracticable at that time of the year, I had to decide\nwhich of the two other roads we were to take, the road by Drangtse (map Tankse), or\nthat by Phuga. As regards the Drangtse road, it attracted me much on account of a description Dr. Shawe had given me of it. The Phuga road, on the other hand, would take\nus to rGya, the antiquities of which I had previously examined. I decided for the latter\nroute, but I will quote Dr. Shawe’s letter on the Drangtse road to show the reader what\nwe missed. He says in his letter of the 19th July 1906 ; —\n\n“ I was told yesterday by one of the men that at Sakti you only visited the newest of\nthe three old- castles — the oldest being a mile or two up the valley. I am sorry I did\nnot know when there. I saw few, if any, rock carvings in Sakti, except a migmmig (see\np. 67) on a boulder. At Drangtse is an old castle and village on top of a rock, destroyed\nby the Dogras. It is in very fair preservation, some of the streets being quite recognisable.\nAround Drangtse are numbers —thousands— of rock carvings of the usual ibex and yak\ntype, but no Indian buHs, as far as I saw. At first I thought there were no inscriptions,\nand nobody could or would tell of any ; but later, on top of a large rock or boulder, I found\na number of carvings of some of which I enclose original copies. One, a ehorten, had a\nlong inscription beneath in letters which appear to be mostly, but not entirely, Tibetan,\nand on another boulder a line in Persian characters. Two or three carvings of crosses\n\n^ J UtMuhco and p. 240 .\n\nwere rather interesting ; I give copies. Another carving about a mile out, on the road to\nPangkong (lake) of a stag hunt, thus [drawing]. A large and rough outline of\nBuddha on a rock seems to be fairly new— newer than some chortens on the same rock.\nI found no kings’ names or votive inscriptions on manis at Drangtse, and the clay tablets\nwere all of the chorten type, without letters, as far as I could see. Ohushol yielded nothing\nof antiquarian interest, and I found nothing more till I got to Nyoma on the Indus. ”"

  "passage_text": "Let me now add a few notes on Dr. Shawe’s most valuable observations. I may\nremark that he was the first traveller w^ho ever passed through this district with\nhis eyes open to objects of archaeological value. In 1906, 1 had travelled with Dr. Shawe\nas far as Chemre {IGe-hde) where we had investigated the monastery built by Seng-gernam-rgyal. We became thoroughly convinced that there had existed a monastery\npreviously on the same site. I went up the valley from Chemre to Sakti on a hurried visit,\nand as Dr. Shawe points out, in his letter, visited only the latest of three ancient castles.\nThe first European traveller who visited the Chemre-Sakti valley, was Moororoft in 1820.\nHe also noticed the “ fort ” of Sakti which was already in ruins in his time. What he\nsaw was also “ the newest of the three old castles. ” Thus, the two older ones still remain\nto be investigated. Moorcroft^ says : “ On the face of the mountain, forming part of the\neastern limit of the valley, stood the fort of Sakti, a pile of buildings surrounded by a\nwall and towers, the whole built of granite blocks cemented with clay ; the houses were\nunroofed, but the walls were mostly standing. This fortress was evidently intended to\ncommand the northern entrance of the valley, but it was taken and dismantled by the\nKalmaks nearly two centuries ago and has never been repaired. ”\n\nThe Kalmaks who dismantled this fortress, were evidently the Mongols and Lhasa\nTibetans under Thse-dbang of Galdan, who after having beaten the Ladakhis in the\nbattle of Zhamarting, besieged them in the fortress of Basgo. On their way to Basgo,\n1646, they probably destroyed all the fortresses of eastern Ladakh, As we learn from\nMoorcroft, the Chemre-Sakti valley was under the command of the famous Ladakhi minister Bang-kha who ruled over seventy villages. The family of these Bang-khas evidently\nhad the hereditary office of ‘defender of the eastern gates of Ladakh. Their principal\ncastle was the gSer-khri-mkhar of Igu, in the neighbouring valley, where there are many\nancient ruins, among them walls with frescoes in front of huge carvings of Bodhisattvas.\nOne of the great generals of bDe-ldanr nam-rgyal (c.l630 A.D.) was a Bang-kha-pa\nfrom Igu. We also find a Bang-kha-pa in a high position of command during the\nfirst part of the Dogra war, when he did not quite justify the confidence placed in him.\n\nAs regards the other places of archaeological interest mentioned by Dr. Shawe,\nthey were not noticed by Trebeck on his way to the Pangkong lake. But Trebeok\ngives an interesting description of a festival he witnessed at Drangtse. As regards\nthe inscription “ mostly, but not entirely Tibetan, ” Dr. Shawe’s copy of it was sent\nto Dr. Vogel, who said that it probably dated from c. 700 — 900 A.D., judging by the form\nof the characters used. It contained the Buddhist formula Ve dharnM, etc., which.\n\ni2\n\n1 Travels, Yol* 1, p 426.\n\naccording to my obseiTations, played the part of the Oni mdtii pctchne fiiuh among the\nLadakhi Buddhists of those times. The Indian, characters, used by them, bear a\nremarkable resemblance to the Tibetan characters, for \"v^'kich reason 1 ha^ e come to the\nconclusion that the Tibetan script was developed in the western parts of Tibet, probably\nunder the influence of Kashmir and Turkestan Buddhism.^ This inscription may\npossibly give a clue to the date of the Maltese crosses found by Dr. Shawc in the\nvicinity.^ Christianity in its Nestorian form was somewhat powerful in Turkestan\nabout 900 A.D. and, although I do not venture to assert that there -aas a Christian community at Drangtse in those days, I think it not imj)robable that tlie ancient\ninhabitants of Drangtse had become acquainted with Christian lorms ol crosses.\nIt is very probable that trade connections between Ladakh and Tui-kestan (.‘xistod\nas early as 700-900 A.D. The Ladakhis were jn-obably ready to try the ojficacy\nof the Christian crosses for the sake of exj)criment, just as they swallow pages of\nChristian books nowadays, if swallowed pages of Buddhist writings have not the desired\neffect.\n\nI was told that there was another deserted Mon settlement above Xyoma on the hd't\nbank of the Indus. When our caravan started for Phuga on Monday the 16th August,\nI made a special trip to this old site which is called Staglung. On my way thither I\npassed by the village of Ngod (JfwcZ, or Mad of the maps) on the right hank of the\nIndus, which is known for its monastery. I was told that the Ngod nionast(‘ry was of\nmore recent date than the Nyoma one, and that it was erected by Xgag-dliung-rnumrgyal, the step-brother of Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal who had been ol)liged to tak(^ n.digious\norders. Staglung is about seven miles distant from Nyoma (or better Xidar) and is\nsituated in a very dry side valley near the Indus. There I found a rocky hill covtu-ed\nwith ruins of houses, the single rooms of which were very small. As there arc* no traces\nof ancient flelds round about, it is probable that Staglung was not a village, but a monastery. Below the rock is a number of ancient mchod'Hen (about 15 to 20) and several\nrows of 108 small mchod-rten, all of which are built of sun-dried bricks. In two of\nthe larger mchod-rten we found cremation tablets of clay, painted red. Two of them\ncontained an inscription of the Ye dharmd formula in an ancient type of Tibetan\ncharacter. When Moorcroft halted here in 1820, the whole population of this little village, who had never\nseen a European before, fled in terror, leaving their houses empty.\n\nWhat may be called the necropolis of the ancient Mons of Rum-rtse, is situated on a\nplain above the trade road, about two miles above rGya. It consists of a number of\nlarge single mehod-rtm, and many well-preserved rows of 108 little stupas. The present\ninhabitants of Rum-rtse said that all those mchod-rten, having been the work of Mons,\nwere not reverenced by them. The Mons and the Tibetans had nothing in common,\nthey said. Although we examined some of the ruined mchod-rten at the site, we did not\nfind any inscribed tablets in thmi. We took a jdioto of a rather well-preserved\nspecimen of these rmhod-rten which was of the so-called ladder type, as we find if\nrepresented among the ancient rock carvings near the Alchi bridge. The lower pari\nshowed remains of stucco frames which, I suppose, originally enclosed stucco figures\nof Buddlia. This kind of ornamentation is not found on Tibetan mehod-rfen. If a\nTibetan rrtehod-rten has stucco relievos, they represent lions, Garudas and other animals.\nThese are not found round the base, but round the middle portion of the mehod-rien.\nAnother of our photos shows some of the well-preserved rows of little slvpae (Plate\nXXVT, b).\n\nOpposite, and a little below tlie necropolis, on the other bank of the rGya brook\nare the ruins of the ancient castle and town of the Mens, called Bjum-rtse-mkhar, with\ncave dwellings close by. The naost conspicuous building in the old town was a round\ntower of great dimensions. Unfortunately, our limited time did not allow us to visit the\nsite. The rGya district altogether is so full of ancient remains that an archaeologist\ncould profitably spend a couple of weeks here.\n\nThere is another ruined castle (called mBihar-gog'), on a spur in a side valley to the\nleft, between Rum-rtse and rGya. Although I could not trace any traditions regarding\nit, it is apparently of Mon, *.e., pre-Tibetan, origin. Besides, there are many ancient\nMon stupas in various places between Eum-rtse and rGya. The two large mchod-rten\nseen by Moororoft on the road before entering rGya, are apparently still in existence.\nThey are of Tibetan origin, and probably not more than two centuries old.\n\nThe site of the old settlement of the Tibetans at rGya is called rQya-mJchar. It is\nsituated on a spur of the right bank of the rGya brook. From Moorcroft’s account\nit appears that in 1820 A.D., the site was no longer inhabited and that Moorcroft’s\ntown of rGya was identical with the present, which is situated on the left bank of the\nbrook. Higher up on the\nsame hill are several ancient watch-towers. When Moorcroft was in rGya, he found\none of the ancient chiefs of the district still in authority. He had friendly intercourse\nwith this man whom he calls a raja. He says : “ The raja whose name was Tsimma\nPanohik, was a short stout man about fifty.” Of course, there were no kings of rGya,\nnot even a vassal king. The title of raja {rgyal-po) may have been given to the chiefs,\nbecause they were related to the Ladakhi kings. Now the line is extinct, and all\nrecords being lost, I found it impossible to establish the identity of Moorcroft’s Tsimma\nPanohik. It is even difidcult to make out what Tibetan name may underlie Moorcroft’s\nsp ellin g of it. I suppose that the man was called Thse-dbang Phun-thsogs, pronounced\nTsewang Puntsog. I asked several people at rGya if they could remember the names of\nthe last members of their line of diiefs, and they gave me the following three names ; (1)\nbKa-blon-Thse-bstan ; (2) None bSod-nams jo-rgyas ; (3) bKra-shis (or Thse-ring) bZanggrub.   "passage_text": "Behind the present village of rGya, on the left bank of the brook, there is a\nplateau studded with a number of ancient, mostly ruined mehod-rten. They are still\nheld in veneration by the present inhabitants of rGya (Plate XXXI, a). This is\nremarkable, because many of these mchod-rt6n which are called Jjha-haib-nichod-\nHen, undoubtedly go back to Mon times. And had not the people of the neighbouring village told us plainly that they were indifferent to everything connected\nwith the Mons? The difference may be this, that whilst the Mons of Eum-rtse\ndid not succumb to Tibetan influences, the Mons of rGya did. We found several\ntypes of cremation tablets with Indian inscriptions, containing the Te dharma formula. The characters employed are of c. 700 — 900 A.H. according to Hr. Yogel’s\nestimate. But there were also several tablets which showed the same formula in\nTibetan characters. The difference between the Tibetan and Indian characters\nrests mainly in this, that in the Tibetan version the aspirated mediae are indicated\nby an ordinary media furnished with a subjoined h, whilst in the Indian version gh,\ndh, and hh are expressed in simple characters. Besides, the Tibetan version has the\ntripartite y, whilst the Indian version has a later form of the y. In two cases, there\nwere two tablets showing almost exactly the same design, but the characters used for\nthe inscription were Tibetan on one of them, and Indian on the other. Among the\nZhd-bah-mchod-Hen, there were also the ruins of an ancient monastery of unknown\norigin, built of sun-dried bricks. I am almost convinced that the town of rGya is mentioned in the time of King Sadna legs, c. 850, in the chronicles of Ladakh. There it is\nstated that King Sadna legs built the temple of sKar-chung-rdo-dbyings in the province\nof rGya {rGya-sde). This could, of course, also be translated by “ Indian Province ” or\n\"Chinese Province.” But it is very unlikely that a Tibetan king should have built\na monastery in a district, the hold on which was always uncertain. It is a pity that\nthe name of the ruined temple in the middle of the Lha-bab-mehod-rten has become\nentirely lost.\n\nOn the 20th , August, we left rGya for Mar-rtse-lang (map Marsahing), the\nMarsiUa of Moorcroft. Below rGya, we passed by a high lhatho, an altar of the\npre-Buddhist religion, with a few houses and fields in the vicinity. It is the Zaiu\nof Moorcroft, and soon we reached the houses and fields of a small settlement, called\nEong.^ ■ -\n\nWe made a short halt at this place, because I wished to examine the site of some\nancient graves, called Mm-gyi-rom-khang, \" graves of the Mons.” Tke first who told\nme of the existence of these graves, was our evangelist dGa-Phun-thsogs of Kyelang,\nwho k a native of rGya. He had told me that he had been inside them when a shepherd\n\n^ Oa the map this village is indicated by the name of\n\nb. Ruined monastery at Miru,\n\nl3oy. He said that then the graves were quite accessible ; that he went down a staircase and came to rooms furnished with boards of pinewood, on which were placed\nnumbers of skulls. The reason why Moorcroft spent such a long time\n:at Leh was his attempt to arrange for the king of Ladakh’s tendering his allegiance\nto the East India Company. It took him a long time to win the confidence of the\nLadakhi king, Tuntuk namgial {Bong-mb-rnam-rgyaT) and his Prime Minister, Tsiva\nTandu {Thse-dbang- dong -rub). But when they were ready to tender their allegiance,\ntheir offer was declined by the East India Company. How different the fate of Ladakh\nwould have been, had it been accepted. Moorcroft had no doubts then, that Ladakh\nwould soon be swallowed up by Russia, for the Prime Minister showed him a letter from\n■the Emperor of Russia to the king of Ladakh whiclx had been brought there by a Jew,\nsix years before. Moorcroft and Trebeck became eye-witnesses of some little warfare\nbetween the Ladakhis and Baltis, and between the Ladakhis and the Kulu State ; they\nalso saw the seditious placard at Leh, in which the unsatisfactory rule of the king\nwas contrasted with the excellent rule of his predecessor, his brother, who had died\n.young. There is simply no end of most interesting information in Moorcroft’s account,\n.and I hope to be spared to edit the Ladakhi portion of his journal with notes from the\nTibetan point of view.\n\nLet me now quote Moorcroft’s description of Leh, in 1820, and contrast it with the\nLeh of the present day. He writes ; ^ “ L5, the capital of Ladakh, is situated in a\nnarrow valley, formed by the course of the Sinh-kha-bab[/S'myye Tcha-bab, i e., the Indus],\nand bounded on the northern and southern sides by a double chain of mountains running\neast and west, the highest of which are from eighteen hundred to two thousand feet above\nthe plain. I, pp. 315 fE.\n\nIt is enclosBd by a 'wall, furnisbed at intervals with conical and square towers, and extending\non either side to the summit of the hills. It is , approached by a double line of the\nsacred structures or manis, frequently noticed in the journal, and houses are scattered over\nthe j)lain without the walls, on either hand. The streets are disposed without any order,\nand form a most intricate labyrinth, and the houses are built contiguously, and run into\neach other so strangely, that from without it is difficult to determine the extent of each\nmansion. The number, it is said, is about a thousand ; but I should think they scarcely\nexceeded five hundred. I'hey vary from one to two or three stories in height, and some\nare loftier. The walls are in a few instances wholly, or in part of stone, but in general\nthey are built with large unburnt bricks : they are whitened outside with lime, but\nremain of their original colour inside. They are usually furnished with light wooden\nbalconies ; the roofs are flat, and are formed of small trunks of poplar trees, above Avhich\na layer of willow shoots is laid, which is covered by a coating of straw, and that again\nby a bed of earth.”"

  "passage_text": "Some other round pieces of bronze may have served as mirrors, such as are stBl
found in Ladakh. Some fragments were probably the remains of bronze pots.

On the 28th August, three of our Christians went again to the graves of their own
accord. They found many more bronze implements, several of them in fairly good
preservation ; for instance, a can with a spout of excellent workmanship, though quite
plain and without any ornament ; a seal with a cross-pattern engraved on it; an entire

bracelet with a pattern of little circles. Although we could trace decorative designs on
several fragments, there was no vestige of any script.

In addition let me say that fragments of iron implements came to light also, and
that Mr. and Mrs. Eeichel discovered the only gold article that was in the grave. It is
of a shape similar to the mouthpiece of a trumpet, but its purpose is not known. Its
ornamentation is a curved form of the Greek key.

L

u

After this description of the gra,ve and our finds in it, let me enter into the question
of its date and the nationality of the people who built it. As I have pointed out already,
in connection with the rGya graves, the condition of these graves calls to mind at once
the description of the form of burial practised in the “ Empire of the Eastern Women,”
of the Chinese historians. There we read : “ When a person of rank dies, they strip

off the skin, and put the flesh and bones mixed with gold powder into a vase, and then
bury it At the burial of the sovereign, several tens of the great ministers and rela-

tives are buried at the same time ! ” The latter statement about this gruesome custom
may account for the great number of skulls, sometimes as many as twenty, which are
found in a single grave. As the grave contained large bronze buttons, obviously a mark
of high rank, it is very probable that the Leh grave actually contained the remains of
several “ great ministers.” This “ Empire of the Eastern Women ” has been described
in the Sui sliu, a book which was compiled in c. 586 A.D. Here it is called Nii-Kuo.
Hiuen Tsiang also heard of this empire, and a little after his time, we read that the last
queen died and was replaced by a king. The frontiers of this curious empire are given
by the Sui shu as well as by Hiuen Tsiang. They are : Khotan, Sampaha (Ladakh),
Brahmapura (Chamba State), and Tibet. Erom these definitions we may conclude that
the empire comprised the Tibetan provinces of Guge and Ruthog, and possibly Eastern
Ladakh. The empire was a Tibetan one, according to our Chinese authorities, and it
therefore appears strange that the skulls of the Leh grave are not those of Tibetans, but of
Aryans. My explanation would be that it is very probable that portions of Ladakh were
for a time at least included in this empire. The value of our grave finds lies in this that
they afford us a glimpse of the general state of civilisation which prevailed in this empire. As regards its date, the presence of iron besides bronze precludes the fixing of any
very early date, say before the Christian era. The absence of any form of writing in the
grave would perhaps point to a time earlier than 586 A.D., at which time, according
to the Chinese, the Indian characters were used in the empire. In my opinion the grave
dates from between 1 and 500 A.D.

Eortunately for me, I had finished my investigations, when Mr. Chatterji, Director
of Archseology in the Kashmir State, arrived in Leh with the message that it was the
wish of the Maharaja that no further excavations of any kind should be undertaken in
Kashmir State territory.

The village of Skara {aQa-ra in native documents) is situated south of Leh and forms
a kind of suburb of that- town. On the 3rd September, I visited the ruins of the
sGar-rtse Monastery at Skara. According to K. Marx this is the monastery " for four
lamas only,” founded by King ’aBum-lde, about 500 years ago. It was built on
a crag resembling an elephant. This little monastery was destroyed by the Dogras, at
least so I was told. There was also another small temple erected below the ruin
occupied by one lama who belongs to -the ’aBrug-pa order. Ho tradition regarding
King " aBum-lde has been preserved in the locality.

The village of Skara was formerly situated on a rocky spur to the right of the
Leh valley, where there are still many ruined houses. The chief reason for evacuating

the former site was said to be an epidemic. There are still many grayes in a side-valley
near it.

Probably the most ancient monastery at Skara is the one which is situated in a little
ravine, between the rGar-rtse iMonastery and the ruined village. Pour walls are still
standing, and there are traces of red colour (frescoes) on the walls. Close by is an
underground room, in which we found a human skeleton of recent date.

Below this ruined monastery, there is a mchod-rten shaped like a “ Mon mchod-rten.^'
It consists of a lower square room, on the top of which is placed a round pyramid.
Locally this mchod-rten is known as the grave of a king. It actually contained human
bones, notably fragments of a skull.

Not far from it, on the plain, there is a group of three ancient-looking mchod-rten
of the usual shape. A man from Skara had extracted from them several ancient household utensils filled with grain. Out of these, he sold me a sieve cup made of very thin
copper leaf.

At Skara my attention was drawn to a rather modern-looking round mchod-rten
which was hollow and furnished with a door. Inside of it w’^e found several cremation
tablets of ancient style, some with Indian inscriptions. I was told that a few years ago
an ancient mchod-rten was deslroyed by a Muhammadan who built a house for himself
at Skara. He carried all the tablets found in the old mchod-oden to the new one and
hid them there. In the desert below Skara, there are the low mounds of several ancient
mchod-rten. We found in them cremation tablets with Indian legends, very much like
those at rGya."

There is no wall on the west side. Perhaps it was left\nincomplete. I made a plan of it. I was told that in the days of the Ladakhi kings (no\npersona] name could be remembered) two men were ordered to erect this temple as a\npunishment for some crime. No woodwork remains, and there are no traces of images\nor frescoes on the site.\n\nIn the desert east of Leh, there is a large mchod-rten of yellow colour, which is\ncalled Ma-^i-gser-mo. Popular tradition asserts that it is one of the most ancient here.\nOn the western side of the dome there is a niche with a complete figure of a seated\nBuddha. It must formerly have had such niches on all four sides. Attached to it are\ntwo or three mchod-rten of more recent date. One of them was open, and contained\nall sorts of old rubbish, viz., fragments of idols, pages of books, charms, and cremation\ntablets. We took away some of the better preserved tablets. In 1906 we obtained from\nthe same mchod-rten a few sheets of manuscript in a modern Indian dialect which were\nsent to Dr. Vogel, for examination. As King Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal (c. 1600 A.D.) exhibited\nstrong sympathies with the religions of India, the manuscripts may date from his time.\nOf more recent date are the pages of a Sanskrit book in D§vanagari character. This book\nused by the Dogras after the wars, 1834i— 1842 A.D., when they established a\n\n£ %\n\nwas\n\nSanskrit school at Leli ; but the school soon came to an end, and the book was then\nplaced in this mchod-rten. mQhod-rtens of this kind, which serve chiefly as receptacles\nfor old and useless manuscripts, remind me strongly of the Jewish Genizas.\n\nThe hill behind the town of Leh is called rNam-rgyal-rtse-mo. On the top there\nare the ruins of the royal palace which was built by bKra-shis-rnam-rgyal (c. 1520 A.D.)\nAs I had often visited this site during my former stay at Leh, I had not intended to\nvisit it again on this occasion. Owing, however, to the return of the Italian, Dr. iFilipo\nde Lilipi, of the Duke of Abruzzi’s mountaineering expedition, with his wife and\nbrother, it was decided to show them some of the sights of Loh. One forenoon was\naccordingly set apart for a trip to the top of rNam-rgyal-rts6-mo, Hr. Eeichcl of the\nMoravian Mission accompanying us. I had no reason to regret having been of\nthe party, for on this occasion I noticed a few things which I had overlooked before.\n\nThe Maitreya temple on the rNam-rgyal-rtse-mo is apparently the oldest, and is in\nall probability identical with the “ Red College ” built by King ’aBunr-ldc, 500 years\nago. It contains an inscription in praise of the reformer bTsong-kha-pa ; and, among\nmany other frescoes, a picture of the bKra-shis-lhun-po Monastery in Tibet. Tliis picture\nshows the group of buildings which make up the large moirastery, and there is a long\ninscription attached to it which is distributed all over the picture. Although this inscription, as well as the other one, is in very bad preservation, several sentences can be\nmade out. As masons or architects are therein mentioned, it proba])ly refers to a\nrestoration of the temple. The name of a great minister, Phyag-rdor, is given in one of\nthe inscriptions. He is possibly the same minister Phyag-rdor who is mentioned in\nthe Daru rook inscription. This is the very one which was erected by\nMug bKra-shis-rnam-rgyal c. 400 years ago, as stated in the chronicles. K. Mai’x was\nassured of its existence by bKra-shis-btsan-phel, his lama friend, but he was unable\nto visit it. It contains very artistically executed figures of “the four Loi’ds” which\nare about from three to eight feet high. The princij)al figm’e represents rXam-thos-sras\n(Vai^ravana). All four figures were covered with blankets ; but these were removed\nwith the exception of the one which covered Vai^ravana. With regard to the latter\nimaffe we were told that it is exhibited only once a year.
